sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether a new fertilizer increases the mean crop yield \(\mu\), given a historical mean \(\mu_0=50\) kg. Classify the test as one-tailed or two-tailed.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: \(H_0:\mu=50\). \(H_a:\mu>50\). This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.
questions.explanation: \(H_0:\mu=50\). \(H_a:\mu>50\). This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a one-tailed and a two-tailed hypothesis test, giving an example scenario for each.
questions.target: The logic of hypothesis testing
questions.answer: A one-tailed test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (e.g. testing whether a new drug \emph{increases} recovery rate). A two-tailed test is used when the alternative simply states the parameter differs from the claimed value, without specifying direction (e.g. testing whether a machine's mean output has changed at all, up or down).
questions.explanation: A one-tailed test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (e.g. testing whether a new drug \emph{increases} recovery rate). A two-tailed test is used when the alternative simply states the parameter differs from the claimed value, without specifying direction (e.g. testing whether a machine's mean output has changed at all, up or down).

questions.q: A test of \( H_0:\mu=47 \) uses a sample of size \( n=9 \), with \( \sigma=8 \) (known) and \( \bar{x}=55 \). Find the test statistic \( z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \).

A machine fills bags with a claimed mean of \(500\)g, with known population standard deviation \(\sigma=15\)g. A sample of \(n=36\) bags has mean \(\bar{x}=494\)g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean is less than 500g, using \(z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\) and critical value \(-1.645\).
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)
questions.answer: \(z=\frac{494-500}{15/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-6}{2.5}=-2.4\). Since \(-2.4<-1.645\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill weight is less than \(500\)g.
questions.explanation: \(z=\frac{494-500}{15/\sqrt{36}}=\frac{-6}{2.5}=-2.4\). Since \(-2.4<-1.645\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill weight is less than \(500\)g.

questions.q: A population has known standard deviation \(\sigma=8\). A sample of \(n=64\) has mean \(\bar{x}=103\), against a claimed mean \(\mu_0=100\). Test at the 1% level whether the mean exceeds 100, using critical value \(z^*=2.326\).
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)
questions.answer: \(z=\frac{103-100}{8/\sqrt{64}}=\frac{3}{1}=3\). Since \(3>2.326\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 1% level that the mean exceeds \(100\).
questions.explanation: \(z=\frac{103-100}{8/\sqrt{64}}=\frac{3}{1}=3\). Since \(3>2.326\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 1% level that the mean exceeds \(100\).

questions.q: A standardized test historically has mean \(\mu_0=100\) with \(\sigma=15\). A sample of \(n=25\) students taking a new prep course has mean \(\bar{x}=107\). Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the course changes the mean score, using critical values \(\pm1.96\).
questions.target: Two-tailed tests for a population mean
questions.answer: \(z=\frac{107-100}{15/\sqrt{25}}=\frac{7}{3}\approx2.333\). Since \(|2.333|>1.96\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the prep course changes the mean score.
questions.explanation: \(z=\frac{107-100}{15/\sqrt{25}}=\frac{7}{3}\approx2.333\). Since \(|2.333|>1.96\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the prep course changes the mean score.

questions.q: Formulate the null and alternative hypotheses for the following scenario: "A factory claims the mean weight of a product is 250g. An inspector wants to test if it has changed (either direction)."
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=250,\ H_1:\mu\ne 250 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=250,\ H_1:\mu\ne 250\). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=250,\ H_1:\mu\ne 250 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=250,\ H_1:\mu\ne 250\). [M1][A1]

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: A sample of \(n=50\) has mean \(\bar{x}=48.2\), against a claimed mean \(\mu_0=50\) with \(\sigma=6\). Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the mean differs from 50, using critical values \(\pm1.96\).
questions.target: Two-tailed tests for a population mean
questions.answer: \(z=\frac{48.2-50}{6/\sqrt{50}}=\frac{-1.8}{0.8485}\approx-2.121\). Since \(|-2.121|>1.96\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean differs from \(50\).
questions.explanation: \(z=\frac{48.2-50}{6/\sqrt{50}}=\frac{-1.8}{0.8485}\approx-2.121\). Since \(|-2.121|>1.96\), we reject \(H_0\). There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean differs from \(50\).

questions.q: A hypothesis test is carried out at the 10% significance level. Find the probability of a Type I error.
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. By definition, \( P(\text{Type I error})=\alpha=10\% \). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: By definition, \( P(\text{Type I error})=\alpha=10\% \). [M1][A1]

questions.q: Explain why an exact Poisson probability, rather than a normal approximation, is used to test a hypothesis about a Poisson mean when \(\lambda_0\) is small.
questions.target: Hypothesis test for a Poisson mean
questions.answer: When \(\lambda_0\) is small, the Poisson distribution is noticeably skewed and a normal approximation would be unreliable, so exact Poisson probabilities give a more accurate \(p\)-value.
questions.explanation: When \(\lambda_0\) is small, the Poisson distribution is noticeably skewed and a normal approximation would be unreliable, so exact Poisson probabilities give a more accurate \(p\)-value.

questions.q: Referring to the coordinate curve shown in the diagram, a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level gives a p-value of 6%. What is the decision?
questions.answer: **Answer:** A. Since the p-value \(\ge \alpha\) (\(6\% \ge 1\%\)), we do not reject \( H_0 \). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Since the p-value \(\ge \alpha\) (\(6\% \ge 1\%\)), we do not reject \( H_0 \). [M1][A1]

questions.q: Formulate the null and alternative hypotheses for the following scenario: "A manufacturer claims the mean lifetime of a battery is 500 hours. A researcher suspects it is less than this."
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=500,\ H_1:\mu<500 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=500,\ H_1:\mu<500\). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=500,\ H_1:\mu<500 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=500,\ H_1:\mu<500\). [M1][A1]

questions.q: Formulate the null and alternative hypotheses for the following scenario: "A drug is claimed to reduce blood pressure by 10 units on average. A skeptic thinks the true reduction is less than 10."
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=10,\ H_1:\mu<10 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=10,\ H_1:\mu<10\). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: Applying Hypothesis Testing principles, \( H_0:\mu=10,\ H_1:\mu<10 \). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(H_0:\mu=10,\ H_1:\mu<10\). [M1][A1]

questions.q: In an applied problem, a test of \( H_0:\mu=11 \) uses a sample of size \( n=4 \), with \( \sigma=4 \) (known) and \( \bar{x}=5 \). Find the test statistic \( z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \).
A hypothesis test is carried out at the 2% significance level. Find the probability of a Type I error.
questions.answer: **Answer:** C. By definition, \( P(\text{Type I error})=\alpha=2\% \). [M1][A1]
questions.explanation: By definition, \( P(\text{Type I error})=\alpha=2\% \). [M1][A1]

questions.q: In the website crash-rate test, describe what a Type I error would mean in context, and what a Type II error would mean.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: A Type I error would mean concluding the crash rate has decreased when it actually hasn't (rejecting a true \(H_0\)) — wrongly crediting the software update. A Type II error would mean failing to detect a real decrease in the crash rate (failing to reject a false \(H_0\)) — missing genuine improvement from the update.
questions.explanation: A Type I error would mean concluding the crash rate has decreased when it actually hasn't (rejecting a true \(H_0\)) — wrongly crediting the software update. A Type II error would mean failing to detect a real decrease in the crash rate (failing to reject a false \(H_0\)) — missing genuine improvement from the update.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the significance level of a hypothesis test, and state the probability of a Type I error in a test conducted at the 5% significance level.
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: The significance level \(\alpha\) is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I error), chosen in advance by the person conducting the test. At the 5% significance level, \(\alpha=0.05\), so there is a 5% probability of a Type I error.
questions.explanation: The significance level \(\alpha\) is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I error), chosen in advance by the person conducting the test. At the 5% significance level, \(\alpha=0.05\), so there is a 5% probability of a Type I error.

questions.q: A researcher conducts a test at \(\alpha=0.10\) instead of the more common \(\alpha=0.05\). Explain how this affects the probability of Type I and Type II errors, compared to using \(\alpha=0.05\).
questions.target: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level
questions.answer: Using a larger \(\alpha=0.10\) increases the probability of a Type I error (the rejection region is larger, so a true \(H_0\) is more likely to be rejected by chance) but decreases the probability of a Type II error (it becomes easier to reject \(H_0\), so a false \(H_0\) is more likely to be correctly rejected) — there is a direct tradeoff between the two error types as \(\alpha\) changes.
questions.explanation: Using a larger \(\alpha=0.10\) increases the probability of a Type I error (the rejection region is larger, so a true \(H_0\) is more likely to be rejected by chance) but decreases the probability of a Type II error (it becomes easier to reject \(H_0\), so a false \(H_0\) is more likely to be correctly rejected) — there is a direct tradeoff between the two error types as \(\alpha\) changes.
